explanation: You saw the real threat, 22. Ne7+ (22... Qxe7 23. Qxe7 loses the queen, so the c8 rook falls), but 21... Ng6 met it by pulling your best piece back from f4, where it was pressing on g2. White then has time for 22. d5 Rc7 23. Qb5, and the c6 knight is cemented while your b8 bishop is buried. Better was 21... Rc7: the rook leaves the fork, covers e7 and hits the queen. After 22. Qb5 exd4 23. cxd4 Bc8, ...Rb7 comes next, chasing the queen and attacking b2. When you must parry a threat, look first for the defence that attacks something, not the one that retreats an active piece.

Pushing 20... c5 saved the pawn but handed White 21. d5, which locks the centre. After 21... Rc7 22. Qb5 the knight lands on c6, guarded by the d5 pawn and hitting your b8 bishop, which is now shut in behind your own pawns on c5, d6 and e5. You are two pawns down, so your compensation has to come from active pieces. 20... Rc7 defended c6 by attacking the queen, and after 21. Qb6 Bh3 22. g3 your bishop, knight and queen keep pressing on White's king while the centre stays fluid. Before a pawn move, ask what square it gives up and which of your pieces it blocks; when a pawn is attacked, look first for a defence that also threatens something.

The b3 pawn was guarded twice, by the bishop on d1 and the queen on d5, so 25... Rxb3 gave a whole rook for a pawn: 26. Bxb3 c4 27. Bd1 and the bishop simply returns to hold f3, leaving you with no attack. Your instinct to play actively was right, but the target was the queen. 25... Rd8 hits it with tempo, and after 26. Qxc5 Rbc8 27. Qe3 Nf4 your rooks and knight swarm around the pinned knight on f3 while the d1 bishop is tied to defending it. Before any capture, count the defenders of the square, including pieces that guard it from a distance.

You are two pawns up and still clearly winning after 19... Bd6, so this is a small slip. The bishop already attacked the knight from c5, and stepping back simply gave it time to escape: after 20. Nc2 the knight heads for e3 to challenge your f5 knight, and White's pawns stay healthy. Better was 19... Bxb4 20. cxb4 g5 21. Rae1 f6. A pair of pieces comes off, White's b-pawns are doubled, d3 is isolated, and with the c3 pawn gone no pawn can ever chase your knight from d4. When you are ahead in material, ask whether a capture simplifies and damages pawns before you retreat.

Rhe8 is a sound centralising move and you are still clearly winning, but it let White's knight slip away: after 21. Nc2 it covers d4 and e3 and White keeps all the pieces on to make things awkward. Two pawns up, the cleaner choice was 20... Bxb4 21. cxb4, which doubles White's b-pawns and removes the c-pawn that guarded d4. Then 21... Nd4 22. Rae1 Nxb3 23. axb3 Rhe8 gives you a rook ending with two extra pawns and a strong centre. When you are material ahead, ask before each quiet move whether there is a trade that also damages the pawn structure; here there was, for one move only.

You had built a real attack here: a pawn up, queen on g5, rook on the open h-file. Taking the knight gave it away, because 13... Bxf5 14. Qxf5+ comes with check and forces the queens off: 14... Qxf5 15. exf5. Your bishop pair is gone too, and White's king is suddenly safe. Better was 13... g6, simply chasing the knight. After 14. Nfe3 Nd4 15. Qd1 h5 your knight lands in the centre with tempo and the h-pawn marches at a king with no h-pawn to shelter it. Before any capture, ask what the recapture does: if it is a check that swaps queens while you are the one attacking, keep the pieces on and push the piece away instead.

Your 27... f5 was solid and keeps you two pawns up, but it defends e4 with a pawn and leaves your rook idle. White can chip at the chain at once with 28. g4 g6 29. gxf5 gxf5. The stronger move was 27... Rd4, which guards e4 from the side and attacks b4 and f4 together. White cannot hold both: 28. g3 Rxb4 or 28. Re3 Rxb4 wins a third pawn, and 28. b5 cxb5 gives it up anyway. In rook endings, before defending with a pawn, ask whether your rook can do the job from an active square where it also attacks something.

Your rook went active with 28... Rd2, a natural idea, and you are still clearly winning, but it left g7 loose: after 29. Rg3 the pawn is attacked and the simplest defence is to retreat with 29... Rd7, giving the tempo straight back. Stronger was 28... g5 first. After 29. fxg5 hxg5 White's f4 blocker is gone, g7 is no longer a target, and your e4, f5 and g5 pawns can roll forward together with the rook behind them. In a rook ending where you are pawns up, ask what the enemy rook can attack next before you send your own rook after pawns; fix the loose spot, then invade.

Trading on b3 was safe and you are still clearly winning, but it swapped your best piece for White's passive bishop and let White win the pawn back: 23... Nxb3 24. axb3 exf4 25. Rxe8 Rxe8 26. Rxf4. Better was 23... exf4 at once, because the knight on d4 makes that pawn untouchable. After 24. Rxe8 Rxe8 25. Rxf4 comes 25... Ne2+, forking king and rook, and 24. Rxf4 simply drops the rook on e1 to 24... Rxe1+. White must spend a move on 25. Bd1, and 25... g5 keeps the extra pawn. Before trading a dominant knight, ask what it is still doing for you where it stands.

You were the exchange up, and 28... Bd7 was a quiet move that pulled the bishop off the long diagonal, where it was bearing down on e4 and g2. It does not even threaten h3, because White's queen on h6 guards that pawn (29... Bxh3 30. Qxh3). The better move was 28... f5, hitting the e4 pawn that holds White's position together and clearing the seventh rank so your rook covers the king. After 29. exf5 Qf8 30. Qh4 Re1+ 31. Kh2 gxf5 the queen is driven back and your rooks invade. If 29. Bf3, then 29... Rf7 takes the f-file. When ahead in material, ask which pawn break opens lines for your rooks.

Your 25... g6 did stop the mate on g7, but passively: it leaves White's queen sitting on h6, weakens the dark squares around your king, and after 26. Rf3 your f6 knight is under fire and you are the one defending. The stronger 25... Nh5 guards g7 and attacks the g3 rook at once. If that rook leaves the g-file, the g7 pawn is unpinned and takes the queen, so White has only 26. Rg5. Then 26... f6 27. Rxe5 Rxe5 28. Qd2 drives the queen home and your pieces take over. When facing a mate threat, ask first whether a piece can cover the square while attacking something, before you move a pawn in front of your king.

Your rook on c6 was the only defender of the d6 pawn, so 25... Rc4 simply left it hanging: 26. Rxd6 wins back the pawn, and after 26... Kf8 27. Rd7 Rb8 your rook is tied to b7 and the extra pawn is gone. Your opponent missed this with 26. f3, but the chance was there. The idea of activating the rook was right, only one move early. 25... Kf8 first, heading for e7, lets the king take over guarding d6; then, for example, 26. a4 Ke7 27. a5 Rc4 works, with White's rooks stuck defending c2 and b6. Before moving a piece, ask what it is guarding right now.

You were still winning after 33... Rce8, and doubling rooks is a natural idea, but it was slow and gave White the one active plan left: 34. Rdd7, two rooks on your seventh rank hitting g7, so that you must spend 34... Re1+ 35. Kc2 Rg1 on defence. Your passed f-pawn was the fastest winner. After 33... f3 34. Ka2 f2 35. Rf1 Re1 36. Rxf2 Bxf2 White has to give a whole rook for it, and 34. Rdd7 is met by 34... Bd4, covering g7 while the pawn keeps running. When you have a passed pawn with pieces behind it, ask first: can I simply push it?

21. Nf6 attacks the rook, but that is all it does: the rook simply steps to a better square and your knight is left unprotected deep in Black's camp with nothing to hit. After 21... Rg5 22. h4 Rg7 23. N6h5 the knight is back where it started, and you have loosened your own king's cover with h4 on the very file Black's rooks are using. The steadier move was 21. Ne2, taking the f4 knight out of the line of the bishop on d6 and queen on c7, so that Nhf4 next brings the h5 knight back into play. Before a one-move threat, ask: once the piece moves away, what is my piece doing there?

Heading the knight for f4 is the right plan, but 15... Ng6 left your b6 bishop loose in front of the b7 pawn. White plays 16. Qb3, hitting the bishop, and once it moves the pawn goes: 16... Ba7 17. Qxb7. You keep kingside play with ...Nf4, but a pawn is gone for nothing. Better was 15... Ba7 first, stepping out of Qb3 and Nc4 in advance. Then 16. Qb3 gains no tempo and you strike back with 16... exd4 17. cxd4 Bxf3 18. Bxf3 Bxd4, while 16. Nc2 Ng6 gets your knight out anyway. Before an attacking move, ask which of your pieces the opponent's queen can hit with tempo.

Your bishop on b6 was attacked by the queen, and you chose the retreat that lets White gain time. After 17... Bc7 18. Qxb7 the queen takes a pawn and hits the bishop again, so you must spend another move on it (18... Bb8) instead of attacking. Better was 17... Ba7, keeping the bishop aimed at d4 and f2. Then 18. Qxb7 Bh3 19. g3 Ra8 defends it, and after 20. Qxc6 exd4 you open its diagonal and also win a rook for a bishop on f1. Your kingside pieces were well placed for this. When a piece must retreat, ask which square keeps it active and cannot be hit again.

Doubling on the c-file to hit c2 was a natural idea, but the rook on d8 was the only thing guarding your d6 pawn, and the pawn on c2 can simply step forward. After 24... Rdc8 25. c4! Rxc4 26. Rxd6 Rxe4 27. Rd7 White's rook reaches the seventh and attacks b7, tying your rook to b8 and giving back most of your advantage. Better was 24... Kf8, heading for e7: the king takes over the defence of d6, so 25. c4 can just be answered by 25... Rxc4. Before moving a piece, ask what it is defending where it stands, and in rook endings bring the king up first.

Taking on f2 won a pawn but gave up the e-file, and your king has no escape: the bishop on g6 covers f7 and h7, so a rook check on e8 is mate unless your d8 rook can capture it. After 28. Re1 that rook is tied to the back rank, and 28... Bxd4 fails to 29. Rxd4 Rxd4 30. Re8#. White then plays Re7 and attacks your queenside pawns while your pieces stand passive. Better was 27... Rd5, keeping your rook on the e-file and pressing d4 and h5; the f2 pawn was not running away. Before grabbing a pawn, ask which file or check your piece stops guarding.

Taking the d3 pawn ignored White's check: your rook on d8 and pawn on b7 were both loose with the queen sitting on a7. After 21... Bxd3 22. Bb6+ Kd7 23. Qxb7+ Ke6 24. Bxd8 Rxd8 25. Qxc6+ White has won the exchange and two pawns with check, and your king is running in the open. Better was 21... Rd7: the rook steps off d8, guards b7, and then 22. Bb6+ Kd6 wins nothing for White. The position was still difficult, but it held together. Before grabbing a pawn, ask what checks the opponent has and what each one would hit.

Stepping to c7 walked your king toward White's queen and bishops instead of away from them. After 20... Kc7 21. Qxa7 the b7 pawn is pinned along the seventh rank and Bb6+ threatens to fork king and d8 rook. Guarding with 21... Rd7 runs into 22. Bxc6 Qxc6 23. Rc1, pinning your queen. Even the best defence, 21... Rxd3 22. Bb6+ Kd6 23. Bc5+ Kc7, leaves your king harassed and a pawn down. 20... Ke6 was the move: after 21. Qb3+ Ke7 22. Bc5+ Kf6 the king shelters on the kingside beside your queen and bishop. When in check, ask which square takes the king away from the attackers and toward its own pieces.

Taking with the king put it on d6, out in front of its pawns, with your queen far away on g6 and White's queen and dark bishop ready to check on the dark squares. After 19... Kxd6 20. Qb4+ Kc7 21. Qa5+ Kd6 22. Re1 the king is still stuck in the middle, the rook has joined against e5, and h4-h5 is coming to chase your queen. Better was 19... Qxd6: the queen returns to the centre and covers b4 and a3, and the king stays behind c6 and b7. After 20. Bc5 Qf6 21. Qa5+ Kc8 22. Qxa7 Rxd3 you are still worse, but your pieces are active. When you have a choice of recaptures and your king is exposed, ask which one brings a defender closer instead of the king forward.

Qg6 took the queen to the kingside while your own king on c7 was the one in danger, and it left White a check that wins a pawn: 19. Qa5+ Kd7 20. Qxa7, when your king is stuck in the centre and b7 is next. Going to b8 instead is worse, as 19... Kb8 20. Qxa7+ Kc8 brings the queen in with check.

Better was 18... Bxe4 19. Bxe4 a6. That trades off the knight eyeing your d6 bishop and puts the a-pawn where Qa5+ no longer hits it, so the king can step to b8.

Before a queen move, ask what checks the opponent has and what each one picks up.

Your knight on a1 was lost either way, so the question was how to use the free move, and 17... Bd6 used it on the wrong problem. It blocked your own rook's file toward d3, put the bishop where Ne4 can trade it off, and left the king on c7 with a7 unprotected. After 18. Rxa1 a6 19. b4, White's queenside pawns are rolling at your king. Better was 17... Kb8: the king leaves the queen's file and guards a7, and after 18. Rxa1 Rd5 you bring ...Bg6 and take on d3. When you are ahead in material but your king is exposed, ask first which move makes the king safe.

Rd7 was a quiet move that left the e8 rook undefended and gave White time to free himself. He can chip at your queenside pawns with 22. a4, or play 22. Bf4, uncovering the e1 rook on e8 and forcing trades: 22... Rxe1+ 23. Rxe1 Re7 24. Rxe7 Qxe7 25. Bxd6 Qxd6, and your bishop pair is gone. Better was 21... Bd5, aiming at the knight that shields his king. Then 22. a4 fails to 22... Bxf3 23. gxf3 Qc8, hitting h3 with his kingside wrecked. With the two bishops and the initiative, ask before a quiet move: which piece can I improve with a threat, and what does this move leave undefended?

The check looks active but helps White. On e5 your knight was guarding f3; once it left, 20. Kf3 stepped forward with tempo, hitting both the knight and the f4 pawn. Now you cannot keep both: 20... Nxh2+ 21. Kxf4 only swaps pawns and leaves the knight stranded on the rim, and 20... Ne5+ 21. Kxf4 simply drops the pawn. Better was 19... Re6, planning ...Rde8 and ...g5, so the knight stays on its central post, f4 is supported and the rooks bear down on e4. You are a piece up and still winning, but before giving a check, ask where the king goes and whether it is better off there.

Your knight on h2 had no way out: f1 is covered by the rook on d1, f3 by the g2 pawn, and g4 by the king. 21... d5 ignored that, so 22. Rh1 simply wins it, for example 22... Rd6 23. Rxh2. The move was 21... h5, which makes g4 a protected square: after 22. Rh1 Ng4 23. Rxh5 Nf6 the knight is safe and attacks both the rook and the e4 pawn, at the cost of only the h-pawn. You are still two pawns ahead, but a whole piece went for nothing. Before a pawn push, ask whether any of your pieces is short of squares, and what the opponent's next attacking move would be.

Your rook on g4 was doing a job: guarding the passed f-pawn. 42... Rg5 took it off that duty, so White can play 43. Rxf4 Rxh5, and you have swapped your most dangerous pawn for a harmless one on the edge. You are still clearly winning with the extra bishop, and offering a rook trade when ahead was a sound instinct. Better was 42... Ke7, bringing the king up: after 43. Ka2 Ke6 the rook is chased from f5 (44. Rf8 Kd5) and your king escorts the f-pawn while the rook keeps guarding it. Before moving a piece, ask what it is defending where it stands; in endgames, activate the king first.

You saw the queen hitting your bishop and saved it while covering g7, so nothing was lost: you are still a piece up. But h6 is a rim square where the bishop only guards, and in the engine's line it trudges back: 27... Bh6 28. a3 f6 29. Qg4 Qc6 30. Qg3 g6 31. Qb8+ Bf8. Better was 27... Be7, keeping the bishop near the centre and your king, ready for ...Bf6 to challenge White's strong d4 bishop. The mate threat 28. Qe5 is simply met by 28... f6, and after 29. Qe4 Bxa2 you win a pawn. When a piece must retreat, ask which square gives it a next job.

Your bishop was attacked by the g3 pawn, and you answered by giving it up for that pawn: after 32... Bxg3+ 33. Kxg3 there is no follow-up check, and you even have to spend a move on 33... Qc8 to guard a6. You are still two pawns ahead, but with opposite-coloured bishops, which makes the win far harder. The simple retreat 32... Bb8 kept the whole extra piece: the bishop is protected by your queen on e8 and still looks down the diagonal at g3 and White's king, and if 33. Qxa6 then 33... Bd5 lets your bishops and queen close in on the king. When a piece is attacked while you are ahead, look for a safe retreat first, and sacrifice only if you can see the move after the recapture.

The check looked active, but it pulled your queen off e8, the square guarding your back rank, before your bishop was ready to help. After 33... Qe2+ 34. Kg1 White threatens 35. Qb8+ Qe8 36. Qxe8#, so you must spend a move on 34... h6, and then 35. Qxa6 can win a pawn back. Better was 33... Bd5 first. The bishop takes the long diagonal towards g2, and the check becomes deadly: 34. Qxa6 loses to 34... Qe2+ 35. Kg1 Qg2#, so the a6 pawn cannot be taken. Before giving a check, ask what it achieves once the king steps aside, and what your piece stops guarding.

34. Kg1 stepped onto the open g-file, so Black's queen arrived with check: 34... Qg8+ 35. Rg7 Qxg7+ 36. Qxg7+ Kxg7. The queens are gone and so is your attack. You are still a rook for a bishop ahead, but Black's d4 and e3 pawns now make the win real work. 34. Kh2 kept the king off the g-file and off the bishop's long diagonal. Then 34... Qg8 threatens Qg2 mate but is not check, so 35. Rf8 pins the queen to the king on h8 and Black is mated in a few moves. Your attack was built well; before moving a king out of check, ask where the next check lands on each square.

Trading rooks on f1 kept you the exchange up, but it gave away your most active piece and let White's king recapture for free. You had 38... Re2 instead, hitting the queen with your rook on the second rank. The rook cannot be taken: 39. Qxe2 Qxe2 loses the queen, and 39. Rxf5 Rxd2 does too. So the queen must retreat, 39. Qc1, and only then 39... Rxf1+ 40. Kxf1 Qe5, when your queen backs up the rook, b2 falls (41. Bb7 Rxb2) and White's king is hemmed in. Before an automatic exchange, ask whether a move that gains time on the queen can come first; the trade will usually still be there.

Your bishop had to leave g8 because the rook on h8 was attacking it, and 15. Bd5 was a reasonable choice that cost very little: it threatened the loose bishop on h1, and after 15... c6 you could simply take it with 16. Bxh1. But a careful opponent answers 15... Bxd5 16. Nxd5, swapping off his stranded corner bishop for your most active piece. 15. Bc4 was more exact: it hits the a6 pawn, so Black has to spend a move on 15... Bb7 anyway, and you keep both bishops for Be3 and O-O-O against the king on d7. Before offering a trade, ask whose badly placed piece it rescues.

Black's bishop on g2 was attacking your rook on h1, and 14. Bxg8 grabbed an undeveloped knight instead of dealing with that. The game went 14... Bxh1, but 14... Rxg8 was stronger still: it removes your active bishop, brings Black's rook into play and leaves the h1 rook hanging. After 15. f3 Bxh1 you would need several moves to trap the bishop in the corner. 14. Bd5 meets the threat directly: 14... Bxd5 15. Nxd5 saves the rook, and 14... Bxh1 15. Bxh1 wins a bishop for it while keeping your own. Before capturing, ask what the opponent's last move attacks.

40... Qf4 put your queen on a square White's queen attacks along the d2-f4 diagonal, with nothing of yours guarding it: 41. Qxf4 simply won it. You were the exchange up with White's bishop pinned on the f-file, so there was no need to offer a queen trade at all. 40... Qf6 kept the queen safe and the pin in place, and aimed it at the long diagonal. After 41. Kg1 Qd4+ 42. Kf1 Re3 your queen and rook close in on d3 and the king. Even with seconds on the clock, ask one question before letting go of the piece: which enemy piece can capture on the square I am moving to?

You were an exchange up, and your queen on f8 was doing quiet defensive work: guarding h6 and the dark squares around your king. 35...Qe8 walked away from that and allowed 36. h6+, a check you could no longer answer comfortably. After 36...Kh8 37. Ne4 the knight joins the attack, and you have to hand the exchange back with 37...Rxd5 38. cxd5 Bxe4 39. dxe4 Rxe4. Better was 35...Be6, challenging White's strong d5 bishop while the queen stays home; after 36. Bc6 Rf7 you take over the f-file, and 36. h6+ Kg8 is harmless. Before moving a defender, ask what checks your opponent gets once it has left.

You are the exchange up with a safe king, so the task was to stay solid, and 32... f5 instead loosened your own king's cover and gave White's pieces something to do. After 33. Rf1 fxe4 34. Nxe4 the passive knight lands on e4 eyeing d6 and f6, the rook has the f-file facing your queen, and the bishop can later check on d5. Better was 32... Re8, a quiet regrouping that frees e7 for the queen: 33. h5 Qe7 34. Rd1 Rg5, and your pieces become active without anything opening for White. When you are ahead in material, ask before each pawn push near your king: whose pieces does this open lines for?

Your rook stepped onto a square where White's idle bishop could hit it with tempo: 30... R7e6 31. Bg4 Re7 32. Bxd7 Rxd7. The rook has to go straight back, and White has swapped a passive bishop for your good one and freed f1 for his rook. You were the exchange up and needed open lines for your rooks, not another regrouping move. 30... f5 was the move: it attacks e4 with the doubled rooks behind it and opens the f-file for your queen, for example 31. Bf3 fxe4 32. Bxe4 Rf7. Before a quiet move, ask which enemy piece can attack the square you are moving to, and when ahead in material look for the pawn break first.

You were in check from the bishop on d5 and stepped aside with 34... Kg7, which left that bishop in charge of the long diagonal and put your king where the h-pawn gains time on it. After 35. h5 Be6 36. h6+ Kg8 you block anyway, two moves late, and White has a pawn lodged on h6 next to your king. Better was 34... Be6 at once: it meets the check by challenging White's best piece, and on 35. Bxe6+ R5xe6 your rooks and queen own the e- and f-files against a bare king. When in check, ask first whether you can block with a piece that offers a trade, before moving the king.

Rh6 keeps you a bishop up and winning, and offering trades when ahead is the right instinct, but it let White's worst piece off the hook. After 24. R7xh6 gxh6 25. Rf1 your bishop is pinned to the f8 rook and your kingside pawns are split. The rook on h7 could have been trapped instead: 23... Be3+ 24. Kd1 Bh6 shuts the h-file, cutting it off from the h1 rook, and after 25. Ke2 Kg8 it has no safe square, so 26. R1xh6 Rxh6 27. Rxh6 gxh6 leaves you a whole rook up. Before trading off an intruding piece, ask whether it can still get out.

Rd8 took the rook off the f-file, where it was the only defender of your f4-pawn, and it added nothing to e6, your other weak pawn. White can go after both: 24. Rfe1 Rd5 25. Re4 hits f4, and after 25... Bc7 26. c4 Rd8 27. Rde1 the e6-pawn is attacked twice and defended once, so 27... e5 28. dxe5 loses a pawn. Wanting an active rook on the d-file is natural, but there is nothing to attack there. Better was 23... Rf6, where one rook guards e6 along the rank and f4 down the file. Before moving a piece, ask what it is defending where it stands.

Your idea of opening the f-file against f3 was sensible, but 16... f4 let White ignore it and push past: 17. e4! threatens 18. e5, forking your bishop on d6 and rook on f6. You must answer 17... dxe4, and after 18. Bxe4 your centre is gone. The e6 pawn is left isolated on an open file for White's rooks, and the bishop on e4 dominates the board. Better was 16... c5, hitting d4 from the side: 17. dxc5 Bxc5 18. Kb1 Rc8 gives you an active bishop and a rook on the c-file facing White's king. Before a pawn push, ask which pawn advance of the opponent's it allows in reply.

Qe3 was attacking your rook on a7, and you defended it by pulling the other rook away from f8, the square where it guarded f7 and backed up the knight. Now both rooks are stacked on the a-file behind their own pawns. White can play 16. a5, fixing your queenside so those rooks have nothing to do, and then open the f-file: 16... Be6 17. f4 exf4 18. Rxf4 Bxc4 19. Rxf6, with the attack on the side you just left. 15... Raa8 simply stepped out of the attack, kept the f8 rook at home and prepared ...d5. When a piece is attacked, ask first whether it can just move before tying a second piece to it.

Taking on a2 wins a pawn and you stay a bishop up, but it ignores White's one real idea: your back rank. Your bishop on h6 cannot drop back to f8 because your own g7 pawn blocks it, so after 30. Qc5 White threatens 31. Qc8+ Qe8 32. Qxe8#. You would have to go passive with 30... Qe8, and after 31. Qd6 the a6 pawn falls. Better was 29... Bf4+, when 30. g3 is the only legal reply and 30... Bd6 brings the bishop home with tempo to cover f8; then 31. Qf5 Qe6 offers the queen trade. Before grabbing a pawn when winning, ask what checks your opponent's queen has against your king.

22... Rf8 took your rook off the defence of e6 and put it on the very square your king needed. With the bishop on g6 covering e8, f7 and h7, your king is caged on the back rank, and after 23. Rfe1 the rook's best move is straight back with 23... Rf6, when 24. Re5 and 25. Rde1 give White the e-file for free. Better was 22... Kf8, meeting 23. Rfe1 with 23... Rd7 and then Ke7 and Kd6: the king walks out of the cage and guards e6 itself, leaving both rooks free. In an endgame, before shuffling a rook, ask whether the king is the piece that should be improving.

You were in check with only two legal moves, and 35. Kh2 walked into 35... Qg2#: the bishop on c6 guards the queen down the long diagonal, and g1, h1 and g3 are all covered. The other move, 35. Rg7, blocks the check with a rook your queen defends. After 35... Qxg7+ 36. Qxg7+ Kxg7 the queens are gone, the mating battery with them, and you have rook against bishop. Then 37. Rd1 e2 38. Rc1 d3 39. Kf2 holds the pawns. You had played well to reach a winning position. When in check, list every legal reply (block, capture, king move) and for each ask what checks your opponent has next.

Capturing on e5 freed Black's d-pawn, and 30...d4! opens the long diagonal for the bishop on c6. It now hits your rook on f3, and your g2 pawn is pinned by the rook on g8. You must hand back the exchange, because the natural 31. exf4 even allows 31...Qxh3! 32. Rxh3 Rxg2+ 33. Kh1 Rf2+ with perpetual check. Your queen on a5 was too far away to help. Better was 30. Qe1, bringing her home to cover g3; after 30...Qe7 31. exf4 e4 32. Rg3 the bishop stays shut in behind its own pawns. Before a pawn capture, ask which lines it opens for your opponent's pieces.

You are still clearly better after 25. a4, being rook for bishop up, but the move spends a tempo where nothing was threatened and loosens your queenside. The pawn now sits on a light square your opponent's bishop attacks, b4 becomes a hole for the black queen (25... Rg6 26. Qf2 Qb6 and ...Qb4), and b2 is left backward. Stronger was 25. Qf2, heading for h4 and the weak dark squares around the black king: 25. Qf2 a4 26. Qh4 Rg6 (stopping Qf6+) 27. Qf4, offering a queen trade that suits the side ahead in material. Before a quiet pawn move, ask which piece could be improved instead, and what squares the pawn gives up.

Qc5 sends your queen to the queenside, where there is nothing to win, and leaves your king short of defenders. After 26...Qd8 the a5 pawn is guarded (27. Qxa5 would simply lose the queen), and Black's queen can swing to g5 to join the rook against g2. In the engine's line your queen has to walk back: 27. b3 Rg6 28. Kh1 h5 29. Qc3. Better was 26. Qf2, covering g2 and e3 and staying close to the kingside, so the rook can take c5 instead: 26...Rg6 27. b3 Qb6 28. Rc5. You are the exchange up, so before an active queen move ask what the opponent's rook is aiming at.

20. Rac1 put the rook on a square the d3 knight attacks. After 20...Nxc1 21. Rxc1 you have given a rook for a knight and made a won game harder to finish. The rook wanted to hit the c2 bishop, but that bishop was in no hurry to move and the knight was already watching c1. Better was 20. Be7: nothing of yours is left on a knight square, the bishop takes d8 away from Black's rook, and after 20...a6 21. Bxa6 Re8 22. Bh4 it heads for g3 with check. Before you put a piece down, look at every square the enemy knight covers; its forks and captures are the easiest to overlook.

Ke6 is a sound move and you are still winning, but it passed up a free pawn with check. White's king on g4 stands on the same rank as your rook on c4, so the e4 pawn is pinned and cannot capture on f5. After 30... f5+ 31. Kg3 fxe4 32. fxe4 Rxe4 you are two pawns up with a passed e-pawn, and both rooks stay active. Bringing the king to the centre was the right endgame instinct; the forcing move simply came first. Before a quiet move, look at every check you have, and ask what a pinned piece can no longer do.

You are still winning after 47... Kg4, and the endgame up to here was handled well, but the king went the slow way. Chasing the h4 pawn takes it to the edge: after 48. Kf2 Kxh4 49. Ke2 Kg4 50. Rc7 White's king blocks your centre pawns and the rook gets active against b7. Stronger was 47... Ke3, hitting d3 a second time. After 48. Rc1 Rxd3 49. Re1+ Kd4 your king shelters in front of its own pawns and escorts the connected d- and e-pawns home, which is the fastest win. In rook endings, ask where your king helps your passed pawns most before grabbing a side pawn.

Trading rooks when two pawns up is a sound instinct and you are still winning, but this trade helped White. Your c3 rook was pinning the d3 rook to the king on g3, and c2 was a weak pawn stuck behind it. After 40... Rxd3+ 41. cxd3 the pin is gone and that weak pawn has become a healthy one on d3, guarding c4 and e4. Better was 40... Rfc4, doubling on c2: 41. Rb1 Rxc2 wins a third pawn, and 41. Rxc3 Rxc3+ 42. Kf2 d5 leaves your rook active with the d-pawn rolling. Before any exchange, ask whose pawns and pieces the recapture improves.

Your position stays winning, and your doubled rooks on the c-file are doing fine work, but 37... Kf5 put the king on an open file that White's rooks can reach. After 38. Rf2+ you must either retreat with 38... Ke6 or block with 38... Rf4, so the king has gained nothing. Better was 37... h5, fixing the h4 pawn as a target and securing g4 for your rook: 37... h5 38. Rg2 Rg4+ 39. Kf2 d5, and your centre pawns start rolling. Before walking the king forward in a rook ending, ask which checks it walks into; when two pawns up, push the pawns and let the king follow behind them.

Your king was doing a job on e6: guarding the d6 pawn. Stepping to f5 is a natural wish to get active, and you are still clearly winning, but it lets White double on the d-file with 35. Rbd1. After 35... Rxb6 36. Rxd6 a pair of rooks comes off and White's remaining rook gets active. Better was 34... Rc3+, keeping the king at home and winning a pawn by force: 35. Kg2 or 35. Kf2 Rxh4, or 35. Rd3 Rxc2. Before moving your king in an endgame, ask what it is defending where it stands, and look for a rook check that wins something first.

Your 45... a2 still wins, but it handed White a resource: 46. c4! Bxc4 47. Kd2. With opposite-coloured bishops, once the c3 pawn is gone the bishop on d4 sees all the way to a1 and stops your pawn alone, so White's king is free to cross and defend the kingside. 45... Bc4 first freezes that pawn on c3, where it blocks its own bishop's diagonal. Then after 46... a2 and Kb2 the king is tied to a1 for good, while your king and the f- and g-pawns advance against a lone bishop. Before pushing a passed pawn, ask what would free the defender, and stop that first.

Be6 aimed sensibly at h3, but it took the bishop off the long diagonal and gave White a free move for 39. Qe5, lining up queen and bishop on g7. Now 39...Bxh3 would walk into 40. Qxg7#, so your queen has to retreat to defend (39...Qg5 40. h4) and your attack on the exposed king is gone. Better was 38...Qe1, keeping the king boxed in. Then 39. Qe5 fails to 39...Bd5+ 40. Qxd5 Qh1+ and 41...Qxd5, while 39. Kf4 Qf1+ 40. Ke3 Bc4 keeps the hunt going. You are still winning, but before a quiet move, ask what the opponent's queen and bishop threaten together.

Your queen on e1 was already perfectly placed: it took f1, g1 and h1 away from White's king. The check 37... Qd2+ gave that up, and after 38. Kf3 the king walks out into the open. You are still two pawns ahead, but nothing is forced any more. The quiet 37... Bb1! brought in the missing attacker, threatening 38... Be4+ 39. Kh2 Qh1#. White can only stop that by giving up the queen: 38. Qe5 Be4+ 39. Qxe4+ Qxe4+. When your queen already boxes the king in, don't check with it. Ask instead which other piece can join the attack.

Taking on h4 still wins, but it pulls your king away from the pawns that decide the game and wins nothing: after 54... Kxh4 55. Rxg6 material is level again and your king stands on the edge, far from d4 and e5. The better move was 54... d3, keeping the king beside the pawns: 55. Ke1 Kf4 56. Kd1 Ke3, and the king escorts them down. If White grabs with 55. Rxg6+, then 55... Kf3 threatens 56... Rb1 mate, and after 56. Ke1 e4 the pawns roll. In rook endings, before taking a side pawn, ask whether your king is leaving the passed pawns it should be escorting.

Pushing 56... d2 let the white king step in front of the pawn: 57. Ke2, and d1 is guarded, so the pawn can never queen and soon drops, for example 57... Rb5 58. Kxd2. You are still winning, but the quick finish is gone. The check had to come first: 56... Rb1+ 57. Kf2 (e2 is covered by your d3 pawn) d2, and now your rook controls d1, so White must give up the rook: 58. Rd6 d1=Q 59. Rxd1 Rxd1. Your instinct to run the passed pawn was right; the order was wrong. Before pushing a passed pawn, ask whether a check first drives the enemy king away from its queening square.

Your move still wins, so this is a matter of a tempo, not a blunder. On g2 your king stands on the g-file, where the rook can check it: 60... Kg2 61. Re4 h3 62. Rg4+ Kh2 reaches the position you would get from 60... Kh2 61. Re4 h3 62. Rg4, except that there it is your move and here it is White's. On h2 the king has no check to fear from the file or the rank, so ...h3 comes in peace, and the d2 pawn keeps White's king tied down. When you step out of a rook check, ask which square the rook can check next and choose the one where it cannot.

47... Rg4 put the rook on a square nothing defends, and White simply takes it: 48. Rxg4 Kf6 49. Ke4 h5 50. Rg2, and your extra bishop has become a rook-against-bishop fight you are now worse in. On h4 the rook was guarded by the g5 pawn; a pawn protects diagonally, never the square straight ahead, so on g4 it stood alone. The move was 47... g4, pushing the passed pawn with the rook guarding it along the rank; after 48. Rc4 Bd8 49. Rc3 Rh3 the a3 pawn falls as well. You had earned a winning endgame. Before letting go of a piece, ask what defends its new square and what can capture there.

You are still winning after 39... Kd8, but the king stepped away from its passed pawn and gave White's rook the f7 square. After 40. Rf7 the rook sits behind the f-pawn and eyes g7. Then 40... Rf1 41. Rxg7 drops a pawn, so you would need 40... Be3 just to hold everything together. 39... Ke6 was the move: the king guards f7 and walks with the pawn. White's rook must go the long way round, 40. Rb8 f3 41. Re8+ Kd5 42. Rf8 f2, and the pawn is a step from queening. When checked in an endgame, ask which square keeps your king beside its passed pawn and keeps the enemy rook from getting behind it.

Pushing to e2 put the pawn where neither your king nor your rook could protect it. After 38. Kf2 the king attacks it and guards e1, and your king cannot come to d3 because the h3 rook now sees along the third rank. So 38... Ke4 39. Rxh6 Rxb3 40. Kxe2 hands the pawn back; you are still winning, but slowly. 37... Rb1 first was the way: the rook covers e1, and after 38. Kf3 Kd3 39. Rxh6 Rf1+ 40. Kg3 e2 White must give up the rook for the pawn. Getting the pawn to e3 with your king beside it was good work; before the final push, ask who controls the queening square.

Kh1 stepped onto the file of Black's h8 rook, so your h2 pawn became pinned and could not recapture: 23. Kh1 hxg3 24. Rae1 Qxd3. Black gets a pawn lodged beside your king and wins the d3 bishop, which nothing defended because your own d5 pawn blocks the queen. You are still well ahead, but it gave back a piece. With only two legal moves, 23. Rf2 was the one: after 23...hxg3 24. hxg3 you simply recapture, and 23...Qxd3 runs into 24. Nxe5, hitting the queen and f7 together. When in check, ask of each reply which enemy pieces it lines your king up with, and what is still hanging afterwards.

You were right to worry about the h-file, but 24. h3 put a pawn where Black's bishop could take it: 24... Bxh3! and 25. gxh3 loses to 25... Rxh3+ 26. Kg2 Nf4#. To survive you would have to give the queen back with 25. Qxg6+ fxg6 26. gxh3 Qxd3, and your big material lead is gone. Better was 24. Rae1, hitting the queen that anchors the attack. After 24... Qxd3 25. Nc7 your knight comes back with Ne8+ ideas, and you can afford to return the bishop. Before a pawn move in front of your king, ask what can capture on that square, and what checks follow.

25. Rfe1 did nothing about the bishop on h3, which was masking the rook on h8. Black now has 25... Bg4+, a discovered check down the h-file; your only reply is to block with the knight, and 26. Nh4 Rxh4# is mate. Taking the bishop was no better: 25. gxh3 Rxh3+ 26. Kg2 Nf4#. The one saving move was 25. Qxg6+! fxg6 26. gxh3, giving the queen back with check so the knight that mates on f4 is gone and you finally have time to remove the bishop, leaving two rooks and two knights against queen and rook. When pieces crowd your king, list every check your opponent has, including discovered ones, before you move.

Grabbing the f7 pawn left g2 unguarded, and Black's bishop on a8 was staring down the long diagonal at it. After 13. Bxf7 Bxg2 your h1 rook is attacked and cannot move, because your own g1 knight boxes it in. The best you have is 14. Bd5 Bxh1 15. Bxh1, giving back a rook for a bishop. Closing the diagonal first with 13. f3 kills that bishop, and the loose a6 pawn then falls safely to 14. Bxa6. You were still winning easily, but this Bxg2 shot at a cornered rook is worth learning to spot. Before taking a pawn, ask what your bishop stops guarding and what the opponent can capture in reply.

Castling was a natural, safe move, but it was slow: your queen on f6 stayed in the path of 9. Nd5. After 8... O-O 9. Nd5 Qd8 10. b4 Bb6 11. a4 a6 12. Nxb6 cxb6, White has pushed your queen home, gained space and taken your good bishop. Better was 8... Qg6, stepping away first and hitting g2 while White's king is still in the middle. Then 9. Nd5 fails to 9... Qxg2 10. Rf1 Bg4, which wins a pawn and wrecks White's kingside. Before a quiet move, ask which of your pieces the opponent can attack with gain of time, and whether you can move it to a square where it makes a threat.

Your 9... Qf4 did meet the threat of 10. Qxf7+ and offer a queen trade, which is the right idea when you are a piece up. But it let White make the trade on his terms: after 10. Qxf4 exf4 your healthy e5 pawn becomes a loose pawn on f4, and 11. O-O-O Nd8 12. Rd4 Ne6 13. Bxe6 dxe6 14. Rxf4 wins it back. Better was 9... Nd8, guarding f7 with the knight. Then if White trades by 10. Qg3 Qxg3 11. hxg3, your pawns stay intact, while 9... O-O also simply covered f7. Before offering a trade, ask what the recapture does to your pawn structure.

White's knight on b5 has no way back: its own pawns sit on a3 and c3, and a7, c7, d4 and d6 are all guarded. 11... a4 fixes that for good, and then ...Ra5 or ...Nd8 and ...c6 attacks it. After 12. Ba2 Ra5 White's best is 13. c4, burying his bishop and giving up d4 just to free c3. Your 11... Ne7, heading for g6, is a healthy plan and keeps you better, but it allowed 12. a4, after which Na3 gets the knight out. Before improving your own pieces, ask whether an enemy piece is short of squares, and take the last one away.

Your bishop and queen were meant to gang up on the pinned f3 knight, but 9... Bg4 left d5 open, and the queen on f6 is a target there. After 10. Nd5 the queen has to retreat, 10... Qd8, to keep c7 guarded, so the pressure on f3 is gone, and 11. b4 then gains more time on your c5 bishop. The better move was 9... Ne7, covering d5 first: on 10. Nd5 Nxd5 11. Bxd5 your queen stays on f6 and ...Bg4 remains available under better conditions. Before starting an attack, ask what forcing move your opponent has in reply. A knight jump that hits your queen is the first thing to rule out.

Your king on d6 stands on the same file as White's queen, so the knight on d4 is pinned and the king is exposed in the centre. 11... Qe8 fixed neither problem. After 12. b3 you have to play 12... Kc7 anyway, and following 13. Bb2 your queen sits passively on e8 while White develops freely. The immediate 11... Kc7 unpins the knight at once and keeps the queen flexible: 12. b3 Bc5 13. Be4 Rf8 14. O-O Qh4 gives you active pieces for the pawn. When your king is stuck in the open, ask which move you will be forced to play soon anyway, and play it first.

Your knight on d5 was pinned to your king by the c4 bishop and attacked three times, with c6 as one of its defenders. 8... Nd4 hit the queen but took that defender away, and White's capture comes with check, so the queen never has to move first: 9. Bxd5+ Kd6 10. Qd1. White has the piece back, a pawn extra, and your king is still stuck in the centre. 8... Nb4 was the move: the knight still guards d5, threatens Nxc2+, and prepares c6 to prop up d5. When a pinned piece is under fire, ask what each defender is holding before moving it, and check whether the opponent can capture with check.

6... d6 is a sound developing move, but it passed over a free pawn. When White's knight jumped from c3 to d5 it stopped guarding e4, and nothing else covers that pawn: 6... Nxe4 simply takes it. The knight then joins your c5 bishop in hitting f2, so White has to castle at once, and after 7. O-O Nxf2 8. Rxf2 Bxf2+ 9. Kxf2 e4 you have a rook and two pawns for two pieces, with the f3 knight driven back. After 6... d6 White plays 7. d3 and the chance is gone. Whenever an enemy piece moves, ask what it has just stopped defending.

The pin on g4 doesn't hold: 12. h3 asks the bishop a question it has no good answer to. Taking is out, since 12... Bxf3 13. Qxf3 puts the queen on the open f-file against f7, with Nf6+ and Rf1 coming. And 12... Bh5 13. g4 Bg6 14. h4 leaves the bishop shut in. So it must retreat, 12... Be6, and White has gained h3 for free. Developing was the right instinct, but the real job was White's c4 bishop and d5 knight: 11... Na5 12. b4 Nxc4 13. bxc5 c6 trades them off, or 11... Be6 at once. Before pinning, ask what you play when a pawn kicks the bishop.

You stay clearly winning after 17. Bxf6, so this is a small slip: you traded away a pin that was holding Black down. Your g5 bishop froze the f6 knight against the queen. After 17...Qxf6 that queen is free and joins the kingside pawns, with ...Nf4 and ...Qg5 to come, which is Black's only counterplay. Better was 17. axb6 at once: 17...axb6 loses to 18. Rxa8, and 17...cxb6 18. Nxd6+ Kf8 19. Nxc8+ wins material while the knight is still pinned and the queen still passive. Before cashing in a pin, ask what the pinned piece's defender will do once it is released; often the pin is worth more than the capture.

Chasing the g3 bishop is a reasonable idea, but on f6 your knight was guarding d5, and 8... Nh5 gave that square away. White can answer 9. Nd5, a knight you can no longer exchange. If you then take with 9... Nxg3, 10. hxg3 opens the h-file for the h1 rook against your h6 pawn, and c3 and d4 follow in the centre. Better was 8... Bg4, developing with a pin on the f3 knight. Then 9. Nd5 is simply met by 9... Nxd5 10. Bxd5 Ne7, and you can castle queenside. Before a knight goes to the rim, ask which central square it stops guarding and what your opponent will put there.

10...a6 spent a move on the queenside while White's pieces were all aimed at your king: the bishop on c4 at f7, the knight on d5 at f6, and the f-file half-open after fxg3. White can simply play 11. Rf1, and castling into it is unpleasant: 11...O-O 12. h4 gxh4 13. Qd2, hitting h6. The better move was 10...Na5, challenging the c4 bishop at once. Even the sharp 11. b4 c6 12. bxc5 Nxc4 13. dxc4 cxd5 only trades off the attackers. Before a quiet pawn move, ask which enemy piece is most dangerous and whether you can exchange or chase it right now.

Recapturing on d5 looks natural, but it allows the Fried Liver sacrifice: 6. Nxf7 Kxf7 7. Qf3+, forking king and d5 knight. To keep the piece your king must walk out with 7... Ke6, where 8. Nc3 piles onto the knight pinned by the c4 bishop. You are a piece up but your king sits in the centre under attack for many moves. Better was 5... Na5, hitting the bishop that aims at f7: after 6. Bb5+ c6 7. dxc6 bxc6 you give a pawn but develop with tempo. Before an automatic recapture, ask what checks and captures it leaves your opponent, especially on f7.

Trading queens when a knight up is a sound instinct, and 12. Qxc8+ Rxc8 13. Nc3 c5 still leaves you winning. But it let Black off lightly: his king sits uncastled in the centre, and your queen was the piece making that uncomfortable. 12. Qc6+ keeps the pressure on. The natural 12...Nd7 leaves the knight pinned to the king, while 12...Ke7 or 12...Kd8 gives up castling, and you develop with 13. Nf3 while Black untangles. Before offering a trade when ahead, ask whose problems it solves: simplify once the opponent's king is safe, not while it is still a target.

17. Qc2 took your queen away from the kingside just as Black's queen and both bishops were pointing at h3. After 17...Re8 the sacrifice works: 18. Nc5 Bxh3 19. gxh3 Qxh3 20. f3 Bxc5 21. Qxc5 Qg3+ 22. Kh1 Qh3+ is a perpetual check, and your extra knight is worth nothing. 17. Nc5 attacked the e6 bishop first: 17...Bd7 18. Nxd7 trades it off, and 17...Bxh3 18. gxh3 Qxh3 19. Ne5 shuts out the d6 bishop while your queen still guards the king. When you are material up, ask before each move which captures near your king the opponent has, and exchange the pieces aiming there.

Taking on f3 pulled White's queen onto the f-file, where it joins the c4 bishop against f7. After 12... Bxf3 13. Qxf3 the threat is 14. Qxf7#, and 13... Rf8 is the only real defence, which gives up castling. Then 14. Nf6+ Ke7 leaves your king stuck in the centre with the knight planted on f6 and b4 coming to chase your bishop. Better was 12... Be6: the bishop steps away from the h3 pawn, guards f7 and challenges both the d5 knight and the c4 bishop. Before you trade, ask which enemy piece recaptures and what it attacks from its new square.

Bd2 is a sound developing move and you stay a piece up, but it leaves your queen and d3-bishop where Black can hit them for free. After 11. Bd2 Nc5 12. Bc2 a5 13. Qa3 Ba6, Black has activated three pieces with tempo and now leans on c4. Stronger was 11. Qa4: the queen steps away from ...a5 and pins the d7-knight to the king, so ...Nc5 is not even legal and Black's play stalls. When you are material ahead, ask before each quiet move which of your pieces the opponent can attack while improving theirs, and tidy that first.

You are a piece up and still clearly winning, and developing the bishop was a sensible instinct, so this is a small slip. The trouble is that Bd3 puts a second piece where Black can gain time on it: 9...Nc5 hits the bishop, and after 10. Bc2 O-O 11. O-O a5 your queen has to move as well, to 12. Qa3. Better was 9. Qb3 first, stepping away from ...a5 and ...Nc5, then Be2, where the knight cannot touch the bishop. Before placing a piece, ask which enemy pawn or knight move would attack it and force you to move it again.

Na5 took your knight off c6, the one piece guarding e5, while your king was still two moves from castling. White could jump in with 13. Ne5!, and then 13... Nxb3 fails to 14. Qf3, threatening mate on f7 and the rook on a8. After 13... Bd6 14. Qg4 hits g7, and 14... O-O loses the queen to 15. Bh6 Qf6 16. Bg5, so you must play 14... Kf8 and give up castling. Your opponent missed this with 13. Bc2, but 12... Be7 and then castling was right: the knight can chase the bishop afterwards. Before moving a piece twice with your king in the centre, ask which square it stops guarding.

Developing the bishop to d6 looks active, but it leaves g5 unguarded, and White's knight, c2-bishop and queen are all aimed at your kingside. After 15. Ng5 you cannot castle: 15... O-O 16. Bxh7+ Kh8 17. Qh5 is a forced mate. And 15... h6 16. Qh5 keeps the attack going, so the bishop has to retreat with 15... Be7 anyway, a move lost. Playing 14... Be7 at once covers g5: then 15. Ng5 simply drops a piece to 15... Bxg5 16. Bxg5 Qxg5, and you castle next move. Before developing a piece, ask where the opponent's knight can jump next and what it would attack with a bishop already pointing at h7.

Pushing 8. d5 at the pinned knight was the right idea, but it left your bishop on c4 where a pawn could fork it with your queen. After 8. d5 a6 9. dxc6 b5! the pawn hits both, and 10. Qa5 bxc4 gives the piece straight back; in the game Black missed this with 9...Bxe4. Better was 8. Bb5 first: the bishop leaves the fork square and adds a second attacker to the pin. Then 8...Nf6 9. d5 a6 10. Bxc6+ bxc6 11. Qxc6+ wins the knight cleanly, with check. Before cashing in on a pin, ask what pawn move the opponent has in reply, and whether it hits two of your pieces.

Taking back on c4 was natural, but it let Black's bishop settle on f5 for free, and after 5...Nf6 Black develops comfortably. You missed 5. e4!, a pawn move that attacks the bishop and takes the whole centre in one go. It cannot be punished: 5...Nxd4 loses a piece to 6. exf5 Nxf5 7. Qa4+, and 5...Bg6 runs into 6. d5 Na5 7. Qa4+ c6 8. b4, harassing the knight. After 5...Bd7 6. Nf3 Black is cramped and has wasted two bishop moves; the c4 pawn can wait. Before an automatic recapture, ask whether a pawn move that hits a piece gains more, especially e4 when it is available.

Your 6. e4 was not bad: it blocked the bishop's line to c2, stopping Nc2+, and hit the bishop. But it let Black answer 6...Bd7, covering a4 and saving the loose knight on b4. Instead 6. Qa4+ forks king and knight with check. After 6...c6 or 6...Bd7 you simply play 7. Qxb4. After 6...Nc6 the knight is pinned to the king, and 7. d5 attacks it; you win it in a few moves, for example 7...a6 8. Be2 b5 9. Qf4 and 10. dxc6. The check also ends the Nc2+ threat. Before a useful pawn move, ask what your checks do: an undefended piece plus a queen check on the same line is often a fork.

You are a piece up and still winning after 12. a4, so this is a small slip: the idea of prying open the queenside is right, but it gives Black time for 12... a5, which chases your queen from b4 and locks the wing. The break was ready at once with 12. c5, while the queen still stands behind the pawn and Black's king is in the centre. Then 12... bxc5 loses the bishop to 13. Qxb7, and 12... dxc5 13. Qa4+ N8d7 14. Ba6 trades off Black's bishop, leaving the light squares to your queen. When you are ahead and the enemy king is uncastled, ask which pawn break opens lines now, before a preparatory move lets the opponent close them.

Your bishop on h3 was already attacked by the queen that had just come to f3, and 11... f6 only answered the other threat, Qxf7+. White simply plays 12. Qxh3, winning a piece. From h3 the queen also guards the knight, so 12... Qxh4 would lose your queen to 13. Qxh4. The move that met both threats was 11... Be6: the bishop steps out of the attack and covers f7 at the same time. After 12. Nf5 g6 13. Bxe6 fxe6 14. Ne3 you are still a pawn up with a safe position. When one move makes two threats, look for a single reply that answers both, and before you move, list every capture your opponent has.

The knight on h4 was hanging to your queen, and castling gave White the move he needed to save it: 12... O-O-O 13. Nf5, and the free piece is gone. You probably feared the fork on c7, but count it out: 12... Qxh4 13. Nxc7+ Ke7 14. Bxe6 fxe6 15. Nxa8 Rxa8 leaves you with bishop and knight against a rook. Your queen also sits by White's king on the open h-file, so he has to offer the trade with 16. Qh3 Qxh3 17. gxh3, wrecking his pawns. Before you defend against a threat, calculate what it actually wins, and compare that with what you can simply take first.

Your knight on a1 is trapped, and 16... Rd8 did nothing for it while taking the rook away from the a7 pawn. After 17. Be3 the bishop hits a7, your king has to step aside with 17... Kb8, and 18. Rxa1 picks the knight up for free. Better was 16... a5, preparing 17. Be3 Bb4, which the pawn supports and which hits the queen. After 18. Qc1 Nb3 19. axb3 the knight at least sells itself for a pawn, and your bishop is developed with tempo. When a piece is doomed, ask before any routine developing move: what can I still get for it?

15. Rfc1 put a rook on the one square where Black's knight could fork it: 15... Ne2+ checks your king and hits c1, so after 16. Kf1 Nxc1 17. Rxc1 you have given back a rook for a knight. You were a piece up and still winning, but that was a free gift. Better was 15. Qc6, attacking the knight, both rooks and the a6 pawn at once. If 15... Rec8, 16. Qxa6 wins a pawn, and 15... Ne2+ 16. Kh1 forks nothing. Before placing a piece, ask which checks the opponent has, and what else each checking piece would attack from its new square.

Your promotion won the rook, but it also let Black's attacked bishop escape with a recapture: 12. bxa8=Q Bxa8. Two black pieces were hanging, and only the bishop on e4 could get away. Better was 12. Nxe4, taking the bishop first. The b7-pawn still attacks the rook and threatens b8=Q, so Black has to block with 12...Rb8. Then 13. Bxa6 protects the pawn, leaving you two pieces up with the rook tied down in front of a pawn on the seventh. Both moves win easily, so this is a small point. When two things are hanging, ask which one can run away, and take that one first.

You were right to stop Bxh2+, but h3 leaves the bishop's diagonal open and gives Black's queen the h4 square. After 17. h3 Qe7 your f6 knight is attacked, and 18. Nh5 Qh4 hits it again while the queen settles in front of your king. Then 19. Nf4 Bxf4 20. exf4 Rg8 21. Qd3 Qxf4 costs a pawn, with the rook bearing down the open g-file. Better was 17. g3: it shuts the bishop's diagonal for good and takes h4 away, so after 17... Qe7 18. Nh5 Rg8 19. Qd2 the knight returns safely to f4. Before pushing a pawn in front of your king, ask which squares and lines it still leaves open.

Your pieces were already set up well: the bishop on g4 pins the f3 knight and your queen and b6 bishop both aim at White's centre. 14...Rad8 was a quiet move at the moment a pawn could be won, and it gave White time for 15. Be2, which breaks the pin. The better move was 14...exd4. After 15. cxd4 Bxf3 16. Qxf3 Qxf3 17. gxf3 Bxd4 you are a pawn up and White's kingside pawns are wrecked, because the trades strip away every defender of d4. When you hold a pin, ask what the pinned piece is guarding and whether you can take it now, before the pin is broken.

Taking on f2 was right, and you stay a bishop up and winning either way; the only question was which piece should capture. After 19... Bxf2 the bishop sits on the square your rook wanted, so the rook never reaches White's second rank, and after 20. Rh3 Rf4 21. Rdh1 Kf7 White's doubled rooks on the h-file give him some play. 19... Rxf2 puts the rook on the second rank attacking g2, with the bishop still ready to check: 20. Rdh1 Kf7 21. Rg4 Be3+ 22. Kb1 Rf8, and White is only defending. When two pieces can make the same capture, ask which one becomes more active on that square.

Moving the attacked knight with a threat on f6 was a sensible instinct, but 15. Ng4 threatens nothing that lasts: after 15...Qe7 the pawn is covered, and following 16. f4 Kh8 17. Qf2 f5 the knight has to go back, 18. Ne5 Be8, with Black keeping both bishops. The stronger move was 15. Nxc6, trading the knight for a bishop instead of retreating it. After 15...Qxc6 16. Qd1 your queen heads for h5 and the c3 knight for f4 via e2, against a king whose pawn cover is already broken; Black's remaining bishop cannot contest the light squares. When a piece is attacked, ask first whether it can capture something useful before looking for a retreat.

19. Qe2 did nothing about the threat Black had already set up: the queen on h3 and the bishop on d6 were both aiming at h2, and 19... Qh2# ends the game at once, since the bishop guards the queen and your rook on f1 takes the king's only flight square. The move was 19. f4, which closes the bishop's diagonal and at the same time opens your second rank so the queen on c2 guards h2. After 19... Qxe3+ 20. Kh1 Rfe8 21. Qg2 your king is covered and you are still a piece up. Before every move, ask what checks your opponent has, and look hardest when a queen sits next to your king.

17. Qc2 did nothing about the attack on your king: the f2 pawn blocks the queen from guarding h2, so Black is a move ahead. After 17... Rf6 the rook comes to g6 with mate to follow, for example 18. Kg2 Rg6+ 19. Kh1 Qh3 20. Rg1 Qxf3+ 21. Rg2 Qxg2#. To stop that you would have to give up the queen with 18. Bxf5 exf5 19. Qxf5. The position was already difficult, but 17. Kg2 held on: after 17... Rf6 18. Rh1 the rook guards h2 and the king can run via f1 to e1. When a queen lands next to your king, ask which piece joins it next and spend your move on that.

15. Nf3 put your knight on the long diagonal of Black's b7 bishop, where only the g-pawn could recapture. After 15... Bxf3 16. gxf3 Qh4 your king's cover is torn open, and 17. Kh1 Rf6 18. Rg1 Qxf2 already costs a pawn with the rook coming to g6 or h6 next. Your pieces on c3, d3 and a1 are too far away to help. The better move was 15. Rae1, or 15. f3, which blunts that bishop and keeps the knight on d2 covering the kingside. Before a piece steps onto a line an enemy bishop is aiming down, ask what you would recapture with, and whether that recapture opens your king.

On e2 your bishop was quietly guarding the knight on f3, the piece Black's b7 bishop is aimed at. 12. Bd3 gave that job up, so after 12...Nxc3 13. Qxc3 Bxf3 14. gxf3 Qh4 your king's pawn cover is wrecked and the queen is already next to it. Only the in-between check 13. Bxh7+ Kh8 14. Bd3 keeps things level. Better was 12. Be1: the bishop steps away from the e4 knight, so you keep both bishops, e2 still covers f3, and Nd2 followed by f3 can push the knight back. Before moving a piece, ask what it is defending where it stands, especially near your king.

14... Nd2 looked like a fork of rook and bishop, but White just steps aside with 15. Rfe1, and your knight then has nothing better than 15... Nxc4 16. dxc4. That trades your most dangerous piece and leaves White's broken kingside (no g-pawn, loose pawns on f2 and h3) with nothing attacking it. Better was 14... Nh4+ 15. Kh1 Kh8, keeping the knight next to the exposed king and preparing ...f5 to open the f-file for your rooks against f2. You are a pawn up with the safer king, so before cashing in a fork, ask what the attacked piece simply moving away leaves you with, and whether your attacker is worth more than what it wins.

Centralising the bishop looks natural, but 16...Bd4 puts it where the knight can hit it with tempo: 17. Nb5 attacks the bishop and c7 together. You must retreat with 17...Bb6, because 17...Bxb2 18. Rb1 c6 19. Nxd6 hands back your extra pawn. After 18. Nc3 and b4, White gains queenside space and your bishop is passive. Better was 16...a5, stopping b4 so the bishop stays on c5. Then 17. Nb5 c6 18. Nc3 a4 clamps White's queenside pawns, and ...f5 opens the f-file for your rooks. Before moving a piece forward, ask which enemy piece can attack it with gain of time, and what else that move would hit.

19... b4 pushed on the queenside while ignoring what 19. f4 had set up against your king. White can play 20. fxe5 dxe5 21. Rxf6! gxf6 22. Bd5, when the bishop hits the rook on b7 with the a8 rook lined up behind it. After 22... bxc3 23. bxc3 Rab8 24. Bxb7 Rxb7 material is level, but your kingside pawns are wrecked and Ng3, Qh6 and Nh5 come at f6 and your king. Better was 19... c4, putting a pawn in the bishop's path to d5 and attacking it before the f-file opens. Before continuing your own plan, ask what the opponent's last pawn move opens, and check their captures and sacrifices first.

Your centre with c4, d5 and e4 is well built and already shuts in the b7 bishop, but 6. Nf3 left the pinned c3 knight with only the b-pawn to recapture. After 6...Bxc3+ 7. bxc3 d6 8. Bd3 Nd7 9. Be3 Nc5 your c-pawns are doubled and fixed, and a black knight sits on c5 where no pawn can ever chase it. 6. Ne2 was the move: on 6...Bxc3+ 7. Nxc3 your pawns stay intact and you hold the bishop pair, and the knight can later head for g3 and f5 while the f-pawn stays free to advance. When a bishop pins your knight, ask what recaptures if it takes, before developing elsewhere.

The check looks natural, but it helps Black: 4...c6 blocks it and prepares ...b5 to keep the extra pawn. You cannot simply recapture, because 5. Bxc4? b5! forks queen and bishop and wins a piece (6. Bxb5 cxb5 7. Qxb5+ Bd7). So the queen must retreat, 5. Qc2, and after 5...b5 the c4 pawn stays. Better was 4. Nc3, then Nf3 and Ng5 to chase the bishop that guards c4: 4. Nc3 c6 5. Nf3 Nf6 6. Ng5 Bg4 7. f3 Bc8 8. Bxc4, winning the pawn back with your pieces developed. Before giving a check, ask what the reply does for your opponent; here it was a move Black wanted to play anyway.

Castling put your king exactly where Black's g- and h-pawns were already heading, with your h3 pawn as the hook. After 11. O-O g4 the f3 knight is hit and lines open onto g1 whatever you do: 12. Ne5 gxh3 leaves you only holding on, and your extra pawn no longer matters. Better was 11. d5, shutting the b7 bishop's diagonal and clearing the way for Bc3, which skewers the queen on f6 against the rook on h8. For example 11...Bxd5 12. Bc3 Qh6 13. Bxh8, or 11...g4 12. Bc3 gxf3 13. Bxf6. Before castling, ask which enemy pawns already point at that side, and whether you have a punch of your own first.

Taking on g4 opened the h-file for Black's rook straight at your castled king, and after 12. hxg4 hxg4 your f3 knight is attacked with no good square. 13. Ne5 or 13. Nh2 runs into 13...Qh4 and mate on the h-file; the only way to survive is 13. Ng5 Qxg5 14. Bxg4, a piece down. Better was 12. Ne5, moving the knight first. After 12...gxh3 13. Bf3 Black's own h5 pawn still blocks the rook, and you challenge the b7 bishop aiming at g2. Before capturing a pawn in front of your king, ask which file the recapture opens and who is already sitting on it.

Your knight was lost wherever it went, so the question was what to get for it. 13. Ne1 kept it for a move but left the g4 pawn alive and your king boxed in by its own rook and f-pawn: 13...Qh4 14. f3 g3 and Qh1# cannot be stopped. Better was 13. Ng5 Qxg5 14. Bxg4, giving the knight back for the pawn that seals the cage, so that after 14...Qh6 15. f3 Qh1+ 16. Kf2 your king runs. You would still be a piece down, but not mated. When the h-file is open against your king, first ask where the king escapes and which enemy pawn takes that square away.

Black has spent the opening on ...h5, ...g6 and an early queen sortie, with no pieces developed. That is the moment to seize the centre, and 5. Bd2 instead puts the bishop on a passive square to guard against nothing: b2 was already covered by the bishop on c1. Stronger was 5. e4, taking the full centre with tempo to spare. If 5... cxd4, then 6. Nd5 Qd8 7. Qxd4 leaves your queen centralised and hitting the rook on h8; otherwise d5 follows and Black is cramped. When your opponent wastes moves in the opening, ask whether e4 is playable before settling for a quiet developing move.

Black's 2...Qb6 was a wasted queen move aimed at b2 and d4, and 3. e3 treated it as a real threat. It defended d4 passively, shut in your c1 bishop and left the queen doing a job, so Black could take a fair share of the centre with 3...e6 4. c4 d5. Stronger was 3. d5: the pawn steps out of the pressure and gains space, b2 is still covered by the bishop, and the queen is left attacking nothing. After 3...d6 4. e4 Nf6 5. Nc3 g6 6. a4 Bg7 7. Nd2 the knight heads for c4 and the queen has to retreat. When ...c5 hits your d-pawn, ask whether d5 is possible before reaching for e3.

The pawn on c4 could not be defended, so there was no need for a check to win it back. 7. Qa4+ let Black develop for free: in the game 7... Bd7 8. Qxc4 left your queen doing a bishop's job, with Black's bad bishop heading for c6 and your f1 bishop still at home. Even after the stronger 7... Nbd7 8. Bxc4 O-O the queen has nothing to do on a4 and retreats with 9. Qc2. Simply 7. Bxc4 recaptures while developing, prepares castling and keeps the queen flexible for e4 and Qe2. Before giving a check, ask what it achieves that a developing move would not.

Your knight had to leave c5, but 8. Nb3 sent it to the edge, where it attacks nothing and has no good square to go to next. Black then develops freely with 8...Bb7 and ...Nf6. The stronger retreat was 8. Ne4: Black's pawns on e6, g6 and h5 have left the dark squares d6, f6 and g5 weak, and a centralised knight eyes all three. After 8...Bb7 9. Bd3 you support the knight and are ready to castle. If Black kicks it with 8...d5, 9. Neg5 lands on a square that pawn pushes have weakened, with e4 coming to open the centre. When a piece is chased, ask which retreat keeps it working, not merely which is safe.

2. Nf3 was a natural developing move, but it left your d4 pawn where the c-pawn could simply take it. After 2...cxd4 Black has swapped a wing pawn for your centre pawn. Then 3. Qxd4 Nc6 develops a knight with tempo on your queen, and 3. Nxd4 d5 hands Black an equal share of the centre. Either way your first-move edge is gone.

Better was 2. d5: the pawn steps past the attack and takes space, cramping Black's queenside. After 2...Nf6 3. Nc3 d6 4. e4 you own the centre.

This is the same lesson as on move 3: when ...c5 hits your d-pawn, ask first whether d5 is possible.

Pushing 4. d5 spent a move on a pawn while you were still a pawn down on c4, and it left e4 without support. Black answers 4... Nf6, and you cannot both defend e4 and regain c4: after 5. Bxc4 Nxe4 Black is simply a pawn up, and after 5. Nc3 b5 Black keeps the c4 pawn and threatens ...b4 to chase the defender away. Better was 4. Nf3, developing with an attack on e5; after 4... exd4 5. Bxc4 you have the pawn back, two pieces out and castling next. In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, ask before any pawn push: can I win c4 back with a developing move first?
